e: `12 > 18` is false, so the first branch is skipped.
`12 > 12` is also false (12 is <u>not</u> greater than 12), so the second branch is skipped.
`12 > 0` is true, so `greeting` becomes `'Good morning'`.
<mark>The page shows Good morning.</mark>

qs.q: Which option correctly matches each layer of a web page with its file type?
qs.e: It is preferred to keep the three languages in separate files: content in `.html` files, presentation in `.css` files, and behavior in `.js` files.

qs.e: An external script is linked by putting the file name in the `src` attribute of a `<script>` tag. JavaScript files use the `.js` extension, and the reference can be placed in the `<head>` or the `<body>`.

qs.q: Which option correctly matches a JavaScript keyword with its description?

`return` — implements error handling for a block of statements

qs.e: `const` declares a block constant. `let` declares a block variable, `for` marks a block of statements to run in a loop, `return` exits a function, and `try` implements error handling.

qs.e: Names can contain letters, digits, underscores and dollar signs, may begin with a letter, `$` or `_`, and cannot be reserved words. `2price` starts with a digit, `my-price` contains a hyphen, and `let` is a keyword.

qs.q: Which statement about local variables in JavaScript is correct?

c.x: They remain in memory after the function completes and can be reused by other code
They can be accessed from outside the function that declares them
They are created when the function starts and deleted when it completes
Two different functions cannot use the same local variable name

qs.e: Variables declared inside a function are local to it: they are created when the function starts, can only be accessed inside it, and are deleted when it completes. Because they are local, different functions can use variables with the same name.

c.x: `undefined`; `this` cannot be used inside an object

`John Doe`; `this` is the `person` object that owns `fullName`

qs.e: `fullName` is a method: a function stored in a property. Inside it, `this` refers to the owner of the function, the `person` object, so `this.firstName` is `"John"` and `this.lastName` is `"Doe"`. The call returns John Doe.

A JavaScript keyword that declares the function `sayHello()` for the button
A regular expression modifier that matches the text `Say Hello` in the button

qs.q: Which option matches <u>both</u> events with the correct situation?

`onclick` — an element has been changed; `onmouseout` — the user clicks an HTML element

qs.e: `onload`: the browser has finished loading the page. `onkeydown`: the user pushes a keyboard key. Other common events: `onclick` (the user clicks an element), `onmouseover` (the mouse moves over an element), `onmouseout` (the mouse moves away), and `onchange` (an element has been changed).

qs.q: Given `let str = "Apple, Banana, Kiwi";`, which statement about `str.slice(7, 13)` and `str.substr(7, 6)` is correct?

c.x: `slice` returns `Banana`, but `substr` returns `Banana,` because it counts one extra character
Both return `Banana`: the second parameter is a length in `slice` and an end position in `substr`
`slice` returns `Banana, Kiwi`, but `substr` returns `Banana` because its length is 6
Both return `Banana`: the second parameter is an end position in `slice` and a length in `substr`

e: Count from index 0: `Apple` takes indexes 0–4, the comma is 5, and the space is 6, so `B` is at index `7`.
`slice(7, 13)` extracts from index 7 up to (but not including) index 13 → `Banana`.
`substr(7, 6)` starts at index 7 and extracts <u>6 characters</u> → `Banana`.
<mark>Both give Banana: slice(start, end) versus substr(start, length).</mark>

qs.q: Given `let text = "Please visit Microsoft!";`, which statement replaces Microsoft with W3Schools even though the pattern is written in upper case (`MICROSOFT`)?
qs.e: `replace()` is case sensitive, so a plain string or a `/g` pattern written as `MICROSOFT` does not match `Microsoft`. The `/i` flag performs case-insensitive matching. The `/g` flag finds all matches (still case sensitive), and `/m` is for multiline matching.

qs.q: Given `let str = "Please locate where 'locate' occurs!";`, what do `str.indexOf("locate")` and `str.lastIndexOf("locate")` return?
e: Count from index 0: `Please` takes indexes 0–5 and the space is index 6, so the first `locate` starts at index `7`.
`indexOf()` returns the position of the <u>first</u> occurrence → `7`.
The first `locate` ends at index 12, then come a space (13), `where` (14–18), a space (19), and the quote `'` (20), so the second `locate` starts at index `21`.
`lastIndexOf()` returns the position of the <u>last</u> occurrence → `21`.
<mark>7 and 21</mark>

qs.q: Which statement correctly compares `indexOf()` and `search()`?

c.x: `search()` supports regular expressions, not a start position; `indexOf()` is the opposite
`indexOf()` supports regular expressions, not a start position; `search()` is the opposite
Both accept regular expressions as search values, but only `indexOf()` accepts a start position
Both accept a start position as a second argument, but only `search()` accepts regular expressions

qs.e: `search()` can use powerful search values (regular expressions) but cannot take a second start-position argument. `indexOf()` can take a start position but cannot use regular expressions. This is why the two methods are <u>not</u> equal.

qs.q: What does `"Hello World".search(/WORLD/i)` return?
e: The `/i` modifier performs case-insensitive matching, so `WORLD` matches `World`.
`search()` returns the position of the match, counted from 0.
`Hello` occupies indexes 0–4 and the space is index 5, so `World` starts at index `6`.
<mark>The result is 6.</mark>

qs.q: Given `let text = "The rain in SPAIN stays mainly in the plain";`, how many matches are returned by `text.match(/ain/g)`?
e: `match()` with a regular expression returns the matches as an Array, and the `/g` flag finds <u>all</u> matches instead of stopping after the first.
Without `/i`, matching is case sensitive, so `AIN` inside `SPAIN` does <u>not</u> match.
The matches come from `rain`, `mainly`, and `plain`, each giving `ain`.
<mark>3 matches.</mark>

qs.q: Given `const fruits = ["Banana", "Orange", "Apple", "Mango"];`, what do `fruits.length` and `fruits[fruits.length - 1]` return?
e: `length` returns the number of array elements → `4`.
Indexes start at 0, so the last element has index `length - 1 = 3`.
`fruits[3]` is `"Mango"` (`fruits[4]` would be `undefined`, because there is no fifth element).
<mark>4 and "Mango"</mark>
`pop()` removes the <u>last</u> element and returns the value that was popped out, so `x` is `"Mango"`.
The array is now `["Banana", "Orange", "Apple"]` (length 3).
`push("Kiwi")` adds the element at the end and returns the <u>new array length</u>, so `y` is `3 + 1 = 4`.
<mark>x = "Mango" and y = 4</mark>
`shift()` removes the <u>first</u> element and shifts the others to a lower index: `["Orange", "Apple", "Mango"]`.
`unshift("Lemon")` adds an element at the <u>beginning</u> and keeps the older ones: `["Lemon", "Orange", "Apple", "Mango"]`.
`fruits.length` is now `4`, so `fruits[fruits.length] = "Kiwi"` appends `"Kiwi"` at index 4.
<mark>["Lemon", "Orange", "Apple", "Mango", "Kiwi"]</mark>

qs.q: Which regular expression performs a global search for an `l` followed by zero or more `o` characters?
qs.e: In regular expressions `n*` matches zero or more occurrences of `n`, so `lo*` matches `l`, `lo`, `loo`, and so on. `lo+` needs at least one `o`, `lo?` allows zero or one `o`, and `l(o)` requires exactly one `o`. The `/g` flag makes the search global.
